questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Controlling and influencing attitudes: propaganda, culture and the arts
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about the success of the Berlin Olympic Games in 1936.
indicative_content: Inference 1: The Nazis had successfully created a positive international impression of their regime. Supporting detail: Source A notes "The Nazis have succeeded with their propaganda".

Inference 2: The games were staged on a larger, more lavish scale than any prior Olympics. Supporting detail: Source A states "the Nazis have run the games on an extravagant scale never before experienced".

Inference 3: The games helped Hitler impress influential foreign visitors and business leaders. Supporting detail: "the Nazis have put on a good show for the general visitors, especially those who are big businessmen".
questions.examiner_tips: Make two separate, distinct inferences. For each inference, quote or cite a direct phrase from Source A as evidence. Avoid simply copying text without stating what can be inferred.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.3: Employment and living standards
questions.question_text: Explain why the Nazis were able to reduce unemployment in Germany in the years 1933–1939.
questions.stimulus:
• rearmament
• autobahns
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Rearmament: From 1935, conscription into the Wehrmacht (armed forces) removed hundreds of thousands of young men aged 18-25 from unemployment registers. Arms manufacturing, aircraft production, and munitions factories created massive industrial demand.

Public Works: The Reich Labour Service (RAD) made 6 months of manual labour compulsory for young men; massive public infrastructure projects such as 7,000 km of autobahns employed over 80,000 men directly and stimulated construction.

Invisible Unemployment (Own Knowledge): Official statistics concealed true joblessness by excluding married women forced out of professional careers, Jews stripped of citizenship under Nuremberg Laws, political prisoners in concentration camps, and RAD workers.
questions.examiner_tips: Level 4 requires three sustained PEEL paragraphs including detailed own knowledge beyond the stimulus (such as the RAD or "invisible unemployment" exclusions).

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The early challenges to the Weimar Republic, 1919–23
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into the challenges facing the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–1923?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Photograph of armed Freikorps soldiers occupying government buildings during the Kapp Putsch in Berlin (1920). Source C: Account by a German factory worker describing the daily misery and loss of savings during hyperinflation (1923).
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Shows the armed military threat from right-wing Freikorps who easily took control of Berlin, illustrating the extreme political vulnerability and military impotence of Ebert’s government.
Source B Provenance: A contemporary newspaper photograph documenting the seizure of power, but posed soldiers may exaggerate their calm control.
Source C Utility: Provides primary evidence of the devastating economic and psychological impact of hyperinflation on working-class citizens who lost faith in paper currency and the republic.
Source C Provenance: Personal testimony reflecting working-class hardship; highly valuable for experiencing the social reality, though specific to factory wage earners.
questions.examiner_tips: Evaluate both sources for content and provenance (nature, origin, purpose) in relation to the specific enquiry. Weigh political threat (Source B) against economic catastrophe (Source C).

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The early challenges to the Weimar Republic, 1919–23
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the challenges facing the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–1923. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 argues that the primary threat to the Republic came from armed political extremism on the Left and Right (Spartacists and Freikorps) seeking to destroy it from the outset.
In contrast, Interpretation 2 argues that it was the catastrophic economic collapse of hyperinflation in 1923 that truly undermined public faith and posed the greatest existential crisis.
questions.examiner_tips: State the core conceptual difference clearly in your opening sentence, then quote directly from Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to prove the contrast.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The early challenges to the Weimar Republic, 1919–23
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about the challenges facing the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–1923. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Source Material: The historians gave weight to different types of historical evidence. The author of Interpretation 1 focused on political violence and military insurrections (supported by Source B on the Kapp Putsch), whereas Interpretation 2 drew upon social and economic records of currency collapse (supported by Source C on hyperinflation).

Alternative: The historians approached the period with different thematic emphases—one investigating ideological paramilitary insurrections, the other assessing monetary policy and working-class living conditions.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that historians reach contrasting views because they prioritise different evidence or timeframes. Use Sources B and C to illustrate the difference.

questions.topic: Challenges Facing the Weimar Republic: Hyperinflation vs Political Extremism
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The early challenges to the Weimar Republic, 1919–23
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the challenges facing the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–1923? Explain your answer, using both interpretations, and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing with Interpretation 2 (Hyperinflation): The 1923 crisis destroyed the life savings of the middle classes, alienated civil servants, made barter widespread, and permanently eroded trust in democratic governance; it was sparked by the French invasion of the Ruhr and government printing of banknotes.

Arguments agreeing with Interpretation 1 (Political Extremism): Violent revolts threatened the state immediately: the Spartacist Uprising (Jan 1919), Kapp Putsch (March 1920) which forced Ebert to flee Berlin, hundreds of political assassinations (Erzberger, Rathenau), and the Munich Beer Hall Putsch (Nov 1923).

Evaluation and Synthesis: While the Republic successfully crushed military putschists via the Freikorps and a general strike, hyperinflation caused widespread psychological trauma across all social classes, leaving a lingering resentment that Hitler later exploited.
questions.examiner_tips: Provide a balanced evaluation of both interpretations. Use precise historical dates, names, and statistics. Reach a reasoned judgement. 4 additional marks awarded for SPaG.

questions.topic: Early Development of the Nazi Party (1919–20)
questions.spec_topic: KT2.1: Early development of the Nazi Party, 1920–22
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about the early development of the Nazi Party.
indicative_content: Inference 1: The party was originally a very small, obscure organisation with negligible funding. Supporting detail: Source A notes meetings held in beer cellars with only a handful of attendees.

Inference 2: Hitler quickly became the dominant, charismatic figure who transformed its fortunes through oratorical talent. Supporting detail: text describes how his speeches electrified audiences and rapidly increased membership.
questions.examiner_tips: State two clear inferences about the party’s modest origins and rapid transformation under Hitler’s speaking appeal, quoting precise textual evidence for each.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: The police state
questions.question_text: Explain why the Nazis were able to create a police state in the years 1933–1939.
questions.stimulus:
• concentration camps
• law courts
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Concentration Camps: From March 1933 (Dachau), camps run by the SS Totenkopfverbände (Death’s Head units) held political dissidents, communists, trade unionists, and social outcasts without trial, creating pervasive terror.

Control of Law Courts: Judges were required to join the National Socialist League for the Maintenance of the Law; the People’s Court (Volksgerichtshof) set up in 1934 tried treason cases without juries, ensuring 100% Nazi compliance.

SS and Gestapo (Own Knowledge): Himmler unified all police forces under the SS; the Gestapo (secret state police) used a network of informers, block wardens (Blockleiter), and wiretaps to create an atmosphere of denunciation where open dissent was impossible.
questions.examiner_tips: Examine three distinct mechanisms of terror: extrajudicial detention (camps), legal subversion (People’s Court), and surveillance/police apparatus (Gestapo/SS).

questions.spec_topic: KT4.1: Nazi policies towards women
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into Nazi policies towards women in the years 1933–1939?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Nazi propaganda poster celebrating the German mother with multiple children under the slogan "Mother and Child". Source C: Secret report by SOPADE (Social Democratic Party in exile) documenting women’s frustration with marriage loans, workplace dismissals, and compulsory motherhood.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Highlights official Nazi ideology emphasizing the "Three Ks" (Kinder, Küche, Kirche), the Law for the Encouragement of Marriage (1933), and the Honour Cross of the German Mother.
Source B Provenance: Official propaganda produced by Goebbels’ Ministry of Public Enlightenment; idealised, showing what the regime wanted people to believe rather than reality.
Source C Utility: Shows the lived reality of women dismissed from professional roles (doctors, civil servants) and resentful of state intrusion into private life.
Source C Provenance: Secret underground intelligence report by SPD opponents in exile; highly motivated to expose Nazi failures, but offers authentic insider sentiment.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the idealised propaganda image of maternal bliss with underground reports of economic coercion and female resentment.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.1: Nazi policies towards women
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about Nazi policies towards women. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 suggests Nazi policies successfully achieved their goals, increasing marriage rates, childbearing, and returning women to domestic roles.

On the other hand, Interpretation 2 suggests Nazi policies were contradictory and failed in practice, as labour shortages from 1937 forced millions of women back into armaments and agricultural labour.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the view of domestic success with the view of economic failure and policy reversal due to rearmament labour needs.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.1: Nazi policies towards women
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about Nazi policies towards women. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Focus / Evidence: Interpretation 1 focuses on early legislative incentives (1933–36 marriage loans and birth-rate statistics, reflected in Source B), whereas Interpretation 2 focuses on the late 1930s Four-Year Plan economic reality and private dissent (reflected in Source C).
Different criteria: One author evaluates ideological messaging and maternal accolades; the other assesses total female labour force participation.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that the authors evaluated different time periods (early incentives vs late wartime mobilization) or prioritized official statistics over workplace realities.

questions.topic: Success vs Failure of Nazi Policies Towards Women
questions.spec_topic: KT4.1: Nazi policies towards women
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about Nazi policies towards women in the years 1933–1939? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Contradiction and Failure): By 1937, Goering’s Four-Year Plan caused acute labour shortages; the regime abolished the marriage loan requirement that wives not work, introducing a compulsory "Duty Year" (Pflichtjahr) for women; female employment actually rose from 11.6 million in 1933 to 14.6 million in 1939.

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Success and Ideological Compliance): Birth rates rose from 15 per 1,000 in 1933 to 20 per 1,000 by 1939; millions of loans were granted (with 25% written off per child); Mother’s Cross awarded prestige; women were purged from judiciary, civil service, and university quotas (capped at 10%).

Judgement: The Nazis succeeded in their ideological propaganda campaign and initially boosted birth rates, but economic imperatives of rearmament completely undermined their ideological goal of keeping women exclusively at home.
questions.examiner_tips: Address both interpretations with detailed historical facts (birth rates, Four-Year Plan, marriage loans, female employment figures). Reach a balanced, sustained judgement.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.4: The persecution of minorities
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about the treatment of the Jews during Kristallnacht.
indicative_content: Inference 1: The violence against Jewish property and businesses was widespread, destructive, and state-sanctioned. Supporting detail: Source A recounts systematic smashing of Jewish storefronts and torching of synagogues while police stood by.

Inference 2: Jewish individuals were subjected to extreme personal brutality and mass arrest. Supporting detail: text describes men beaten in the streets and rounded up for deportation to concentration camps.
questions.examiner_tips: State two inferences regarding state-coordinated destruction and arbitrary terror, supported with direct quotes from Source A.

questions.topic: Economic Recovery in the Weimar Republic (1924–29)
questions.spec_topic: KT1.3: The "Golden Years": recovery of the Republic, 1924–29
questions.question_text: Explain why the German economy recovered in the years 1924–1929.
questions.stimulus:
• Gustav Stresemann
• Dawes Plan
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Gustav Stresemann & Currency Reform: As Chancellor in late 1923, Stresemann ended passive resistance in the Ruhr and introduced the Rentenmark (backed by industrial and agricultural land), bringing hyperinflation to an immediate halt and restoring currency confidence.

Dawes Plan (1924): Reorganised reparations to start at 1 billion marks annually, rising to 2.5 billion, and secured an initial 800 million gold mark loan from US banks; followed by the Young Plan (1929) cutting reparations to £2 billion.

Industrial Modernisation & US Loans (Own Knowledge): Over 25 billion marks in American loans flooded into German industry, funding factories, coal and steel cartels, public housing, schools, and roads; industrial production surpassed 1913 pre-war levels by 1928.
questions.examiner_tips: Cover monetary stabilisation (Rentenmark), international diplomacy (Dawes Plan/US loans), and industrial rebuilding. Note Stresemann’s warning that Germany was "dancing on a volcano".

questions.spec_topic: KT3.4: Opposition, resistance and conformity
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into the extent of support for the Nazi regime in the years 1933–1939?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Report by an American journalist describing genuine public adulation for Hitler at public rallies and mass enthusiasm for economic recovery. Source C: Secret Gestapo surveillance report recording widespread grumbling and cynical jokes about food shortages and corruption among Nazi party bosses.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Documents the very real popularity of Hitler’s foreign policy successes, restoration of law and order, and pride restored to ordinary citizens.
Source B Provenance: Foreign observer with freedom to report, but public spectacles and choreographed Nuremberg rallies tended to mask private dissent.
Source C Utility: Provides crucial evidence of hidden dissent, grumbling over butter shortages, and public cynicism regarding corrupt "little Hitlers" in local party posts.
Source C Provenance: Confidential internal police intelligence; highly objective because Gestapo commanders required accurate facts on public morale.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast outward public adulation at mass rallies with confidential internal surveillance exposing day-to-day discontent and cynicism.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.4: Opposition, resistance and conformity
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the extent of support for the Nazi regime in the years 1933–1939. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 argues that the vast majority of Germans genuinely supported Hitler, grateful for economic stability, employment, and national restoration.
Interpretation 2 contends that genuine active support was limited, and that most Germans merely conformed out of fear of the Gestapo, intimidation, and the lack of political alternatives.
questions.examiner_tips: State clearly the contrast between genuine popular consensus versus coerced conformity and pervasive fear.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.4: Opposition, resistance and conformity
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about the extent of support for the Nazi regime in the years 1933–1939. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Differing Sources: Interpretation 1 drew upon public sources, plebiscite results, and eyewitness accounts of mass rallies (similar to Source B), whereas Interpretation 2 utilized secret police records and underground opposition reports (similar to Source C) showing private grumbling.
Differing definitions of "support": One historian measures the absence of open revolt and high plebiscite votes; the other investigates genuine ideological conviction vs reluctant compliance.
questions.examiner_tips: Link the historians’ differing conclusions directly to their reliance on public propaganda displays vs confidential police records.

questions.topic: Popular Support vs Fear and Coercion in Nazi Germany
questions.spec_topic: KT3.4: Opposition, resistance and conformity
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the extent of support for the Nazi regime in the years 1933–1939? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing with Interpretation 2 (Coercion and Passive Conformity): The terror apparatus (SS, Gestapo, block wardens, Dachau) made active opposition suicidal; the abolition of trade unions (May 1933) and rival political parties (July 1933) eliminated organized resistance; many Germans retreated into "internal exile" or grumbled in private.

Arguments agreeing with Interpretation 1 (Genuine Popular Support): Millions benefited from full employment, Strength through Joy (KdF) subsidized holidays and theatre tickets, the Beauty of Labour (SdA) improved factory conditions; Hitler was personally adored for tearing up the hated Treaty of Versailles and remilitarising the Rhineland (1936).

Conclusion / Synthesis: Support was multi-layered: immense genuine adoration for the "Hitler Myth" combined with widespread passive acceptance of the regime’s social benefits, while open political resistance was completely silenced by the police state.
questions.examiner_tips: Provide a sophisticated analysis distinguishing between the "Hitler Myth" of personal popularity and resentment towards local Nazi officials. Include SPaG.

questions.topic: Nazi Reaction to the Reichstag Fire (1933)
questions.spec_topic: KT3.1: Creating a dictatorship, 1933–34
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about how the Nazis reacted to the Reichstag Fire.
indicative_content: Inference 1: The Nazis immediately used the fire as a pretext to launch a ruthless crackdown against the Communist Party (KPD). Supporting detail: Source A describes police raiding communist headquarters and arresting thousands of party officials.

Inference 2: The Nazi leaders portrayed the blaze as the start of a violent nationwide communist revolution to justify suspending civil liberties. Supporting detail: Goering and Hitler declaring the fire was a "beacon" for armed insurrection.
questions.examiner_tips: Two separate inferences showing political exploitation of the fire to eliminate communist opponents, backed with direct quotes.

questions.topic: Early Unpopularity of the Weimar Republic (1919–23)
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The early challenges to the Weimar Republic, 1919–23
questions.question_text: Explain why the Weimar Republic was unpopular in the years 1919–1923.
questions.stimulus:
• reparations
• the new Constitution
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Reparations: The crushing £6.6 billion sum fixed in 1921 drained the economy, stoked inflation, and led directly to the 1923 default and French occupation of the Ruhr.

The Weimar Constitution: Proportional representation led to unstable coalition governments and frequent cabinet collapses; Article 48 gave emergency dictatorial powers to the President; traditional elites resented democratic egalitarianism.

The "Dolchstoss" / Treaty of Versailles (Own Knowledge): The Republic was forever branded the "November Criminals" for signing the armistice and the "Diktat" of Versailles, which stripped 13% of territory, 100% of colonies, demilitarised the Rhineland, and imposed the War Guilt Clause (Article 231).
questions.examiner_tips: Explain three distinct reasons: economic resentment (reparations), structural political weakness (proportional representation/coalitions), and nationalist shame (Versailles/Diktat).

questions.topic: Support for the Nazi Party in the "Lean Years" (1924–28)
questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: The Munich Putsch and the Nazi Party, 1923–28
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into support for the Nazi Party in the years 1924–1928?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Report on Nazi election campaigning in rural Protestant areas showing growing attraction among farmers facing agricultural depression. Source C: National election statistics and press commentary from 1928 showing the Nazis won only 2.6% of the national vote (12 Reichstag seats).
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Highlights the targeted strategy of winning over rural, small-town voters and farmers who did not share in the Weimar urban boom.
Source B Provenance: Regional contemporary report detailing grass-roots party work, giving granular local insight.
Source C Utility: Provides objective statistical evidence of national electoral marginalisation during the Stresemann "Golden Years" when the public favoured moderate parties.
Source C Provenance: Official election results from May 1928, highly reliable for assessing national voting share.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the national electoral failure (2.6% in 1928) with regional breakthroughs among discontented rural farming communities.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: The Munich Putsch and the Nazi Party, 1923–28
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about support for the Nazi Party in the years 1924–1928. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 emphasizes that the Nazi Party was an insignificant fringe group completely rejected by the German electorate during the prosperous Stresemann years.

Interpretation 2 emphasizes that despite low votes, the party successfully built a formidable nationwide organisation, establishing Gauleiter networks and front organisations that prepared them for future breakthrough.
questions.examiner_tips: State the difference between electoral failure on the surface vs organizational groundwork beneath the surface.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: The Munich Putsch and the Nazi Party, 1923–28
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about support for the Nazi Party in the years 1924–1928. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Focus: Interpretation 1 focuses on parliamentary election tallies (Source C showing 12 seats), whereas Interpretation 2 focuses on party membership figures, local propaganda networks, and rural outreach (Source B).
Different time horizons: One author looks strictly at contemporary political power; the other evaluates the organisational foundation that enabled the post-1929 surge.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that one historian judged electoral impact while the other evaluated organizational development.

questions.topic: Significance of the Nazi "Lean Years": Marginal Fringe or Crucial Foundation?
questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: The Munich Putsch and the Nazi Party, 1923–28
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about support for the Nazi Party in the years 1924–1928? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Vital Organisational Foundation): Following release from Landsberg prison, Hitler re-founded the NSDAP in 1925; at the 1926 Bamberg Conference he established the Führerprinzip and defeated the northern socialist wing; party membership rose from 27,000 in 1925 to over 100,000 by 1928; established the SS and Hitler Youth.

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Complete Marginalisation): The Weimar Republic was politically stable and culturally thriving; the SPD won 153 seats in 1928 while Nazis won only 12; radical extremism had zero appeal to employed urban workers enjoying higher wages and modern welfare.

Synthesis: The Nazis were indeed an electoral irrelevance while Stresemann’s economic recovery held, but their organisational restructuring between 1924 and 1928 was indispensable for capitalising on the Wall Street Crash.
questions.examiner_tips: Balance 1928 electoral weakness against internal party restructuring (Bamberg Conference, Gauleiter, membership growth). Conclude with a clear judgement.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.2: Nazi policies towards the young
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about the Hitler Youth.
indicative_content: Inference 1: The Hitler Youth focused heavily on physical conditioning and military drill rather than academic learning. Supporting detail: Source A highlights rifle practice, obstacle courses, and marching in uniforms.

Inference 2: The organisation was designed to instill absolute loyalty to Adolf Hitler and break parental authority. Supporting detail: text describes boys being taught to put loyalty to the Führer above their own families.
questions.examiner_tips: State two inferences about militarisation and ideological indoctrination, supporting each with a direct quotation from Source A.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Controlling and influencing attitudes: propaganda, culture and the arts
questions.question_text: Explain why the use of propaganda helped the Nazis to control the attitudes of the German people in the years 1933–1939.
questions.stimulus:
• newspapers
• Nazi rallies
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Newspapers: Goebbels brought all press under Nazi control through the Reich Press Law (1933); the DNB news agency dictated daily editorial lines; anti-Nazi newspapers were closed and editors were vetted.

Nazi Rallies: Annual Nuremberg Rallies staged vast theatrical spectacles with searchlight "cathedrals of light", military parades, and mass choral salutes, instilling awe, unity, and submission to the Führer.

Radio and Culture (Own Knowledge): The People’s Receiver (Volksempfänger 301) was subsidized and mass-produced so 70% of homes had radio by 1939; loudspeakers installed in public squares broadcast speeches; cinema was censored and preceded by propaganda newsreels.
questions.examiner_tips: Analyze how Goebbels combined media censorship (newspapers), emotional spectacles (Nuremberg), and modern technology (radio/film) to reshape public consciousness.

questions.topic: Why Hitler Became Chancellor in January 1933
questions.spec_topic: KT2.4: How Hitler became Chancellor, 1932–33
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into the reasons why Hitler became Chancellor in 1933?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Diary entry by Franz von Papen explaining his political deal to convince Hindenburg to appoint Hitler with Papen as Vice-Chancellor to "box him in". Source C: Eyewitness account of mass Nazi political rallies and SA marching through Berlin after the July 1932 election.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Exposes the backdoor political intrigues, rivalries between Schleicher and Papen, and Hindenburg’s elite cabal who mistakenly thought they could control Hitler.
Source B Provenance: First-hand insider account from Papen himself, highly revealing of his hubris and miscalculation, though written to defend his own role.
Source C Utility: Illustrates the immense popular mandate and intimidating street presence of the NSDAP as the largest party in the Reichstag (230 seats in July 1932).
Source C Provenance: Contemporary observer capturing the atmospheric dread and street momentum that forced Weimar politicians to negotiate with Hitler.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the top-down political intrigue of the Weimar elites (Papen/Hindenburg) with bottom-up electoral and paramilitary pressure (SA/July 1932 election).

questions.spec_topic: KT2.4: How Hitler became Chancellor, 1932–33
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the reasons why Hitler became Chancellor in 1933. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 argues Hitler was appointed primarily due to the political backstairs intrigue, selfish calculations, and fatal misjudgements of Papen and Hindenburg.
Interpretation 2 argues Hitler became Chancellor because of his massive popular appeal, the electoral dominance of the Nazi party following the Great Depression, and the threat of civil war.
questions.examiner_tips: State the difference between elite backstairs intrigue vs mass electoral and economic momentum, quoting both interpretations.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.4: How Hitler became Chancellor, 1932–33
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about the reasons why Hitler became Chancellor in 1933. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Evidence Focus: Interpretation 1 drew upon cabinet papers, private diaries, and negotiations between Papen, Schleicher, and Oskar von Hindenburg (Source B). Interpretation 2 drew upon election statistics, unemployment data, and rally reports showing popular mass mobilisation (Source C).
Alternative: One historian investigated the final constitutional trigger in January 1933; the other examined the long-term socio-economic breakdown after 1929.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that the historians focused on different causal layers: short-term elite intrigue vs long-term socio-economic crisis.

questions.topic: Hitler’s Appointment: Elite Backstairs Intrigue vs Mass Electoral Mandate
questions.spec_topic: KT2.4: How Hitler became Chancellor, 1932–33
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the reasons why Hitler became Chancellor in 1933? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Mass Electoral and Economic Pressure): 6 million unemployed after Wall Street Crash drove voters to extremes; Nazis won 230 seats (37.3%) in July 1932; Hitler’s charismatic speeches promised "Work and Bread" to all classes; the SA (400,000 men) intimidated opponents and projected strength.

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Elite Intrigue and Papen’s Betrayal): In Nov 1932, Nazi votes fell to 196 seats and the party was bankrupt; Hitler did not seize power—he was handed it by Papen and Hindenburg to oust General Schleicher; Papen boasted "we have hired him" with only 3 Nazis in a cabinet of 12.

Synthesis: Mass popularity created the indispensable prerequisite (Hitler could not be ignored), but elite political intrigue was the immediate spark that unlocked the Chancellorship when the Nazi movement was actually losing momentum.
questions.examiner_tips: Critically assess the interaction between mass electoral popularity and elite political intrigue. Note the November 1932 drop in Nazi votes to demonstrate that intrigue was decisive.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.2: Nazi policies towards the young
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about education in Nazi Germany.
indicative_content: Inference 1: School curricula were heavily rewritten to promote racial ideology and anti-Semitism. Supporting detail: Source A references biology lessons centered on eugenics and racial purity.
Inference 2: Teachers were forced to conform to Nazi ideology or face dismissal. Supporting detail: text mentions mandatory membership in the National Socialist Teachers’ League (NSLB).
questions.examiner_tips: Identify two distinct inferences about curriculum Nazification and teacher conformity, citing exact evidence from the text.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: The Munich Putsch and the Nazi Party, 1923–28
questions.question_text: Explain why the Nazi Party was reorganised in the years 1924–1928.
questions.stimulus:
• elections
• the Bamberg Conference (1926)
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Legal Path to Power after Munich Putsch (Elections): The failure of the 1923 Putsch convinced Hitler that armed revolution was impossible; the party had to win power legally through Reichstag elections, requiring a structured electoral machine.

The Bamberg Conference (1926): Hitler re-established his supreme authority (Führerprinzip), sidelined Gregor Strasser’s socialist wing, and unified party ideology behind anti-Semitism and anti-communism.

National Structure & Propaganda (Own Knowledge): Germany was divided into 35 Gau regions led by loyal Gauleiters; specialised front organisations were established (SS, Hitler Youth, Nazi Teachers’ League) to broaden appeal across different demographic groups.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain why structural change was needed: strategic shift from putsch to legal elections, asserting the Führerprinzip at Bamberg, and establishing nationwide Gauleiter apparatus.

questions.topic: Cultural Changes in the Weimar Republic (1924–29)
questions.spec_topic: KT1.4: Changes in society, 1924–29: Cultural changes
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into cultural changes in the Weimar Republic in the years 1924–1929?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Photograph of a Bauhaus architectural design exhibition in Dessau celebrating modernist minimalism and functional technology. Source C: Right-wing nationalist article condemning Berlin cabaret culture, American jazz music, and "degenerate" avant-garde art.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Shows the pioneering artistic innovations of the Bauhaus movement under Walter Gropius, reflecting Weimar’s spirit of experimentation and modernism.
Source B Provenance: An architectural promotional photograph highlighting modernist achievements; limited to urban avant-garde designers.
Source C Utility: Demonstrates the deep conservative, traditionalist backlash against Weimar modernism, viewed by rural and right-wing Germans as moral decay.
Source C Provenance: Nationalist publication designed to inflame public anger against the Republic’s cultural freedom.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the exciting avant-garde innovations of Weimar culture (Bauhaus/cabaret) with the fierce conservative hostility it provoked across provincial Germany.

questions.topic: Cultural Changes in the Weimar Republic (1924–29)
questions.spec_topic: KT1.4: Changes in society, 1924–29: Cultural changes
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about cultural changes in the Weimar Republic in the years 1924–1929. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 portrays the 1920s as a vibrant "Golden Age" of artistic freedom, creativity, and world-leading culture.
Interpretation 2 argues that cultural experimentation was confined to a small Berlin elite and provoked deep moral outrage and disgust among the majority of ordinary Germans.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the celebratory view of a vibrant cultural renaissance with the critical view of cultural division and public alienation.

questions.topic: Cultural Changes in the Weimar Republic (1924–29)
questions.spec_topic: KT1.4: Changes in society, 1924–29: Cultural changes
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about cultural changes in the Weimar Republic in the years 1924–1929. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Focus / Geography: Interpretation 1 focused on Berlin’s avant-garde art, cinema (Fritz Lang’s Metropolis), and Bauhaus architecture (Source B). Interpretation 2 drew upon conservative, rural publications and church complaints (Source C) protesting moral decline.
Different evaluative criteria: One assesses artistic innovation; the other assesses societal cohesion and electoral impact.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that the authors focused on different locations (cosmopolitan Berlin vs conservative countryside) and different social groups.

questions.topic: Weimar Culture: Golden Age of Innovation or Source of Political Polarization?
questions.spec_topic: KT1.4: Changes in society, 1924–29: Cultural changes
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about cultural changes in the Weimar Republic in the years 1924–1929? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Alienation and Conservative Backlash): The new culture was largely restricted to metropolitan centers like Berlin; traditional middle classes and rural Catholics were horrified by nudism, cabaret decadence, and American jazz; nationalists branded it "cultural Bolshevism" and used it as powerful propaganda against democracy.

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Golden Age of Innovation): Article 118 guaranteed free expression; Germany led the world in cinema (Marlene Dietrich in The Blue Angel, Nosferatu), literature (Remarque’s All Quiet on the Western Front), art (George Grosz, Otto Dix), and architecture (Bauhaus Dessau).

Judgement: Weimar culture was undeniably brilliant in its creativity, but by alienating conservative, religious, and rural Germans, it deepened political divisions and provided fertile ground for Nazi propaganda.
questions.examiner_tips: Synthesise both views: brilliant artistic freedom existed alongside deep societal polarization that undermined the Republic’s stability.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.1: Early development of the Nazi Party, 1920–22
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about how Hitler increased support for the Nazi Party in the early 1920s.
indicative_content: Inference 1: Hitler used powerful emotional oratory and targeted grievances to captivate beer hall audiences. Supporting detail: Source A recounts how his passionate delivery resonated with angry war veterans.
Inference 2: The party created striking visual branding and propaganda symbols. Supporting detail: text notes the swastika emblem, party banners, and energetic SA presence attracting attention.
questions.examiner_tips: State two clear inferences regarding Hitler’s oratorical appeal and party branding/SA street visibility, citing Source A quotes.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The early challenges to the Weimar Republic, 1919–23
questions.question_text: Explain why the situation in Germany was unstable in the years 1918–1923.
questions.stimulus:
• the Spartacist revolt
• hyperinflation
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: The Spartacist Revolt (Left-Wing Threat): In January 1919, Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht led a communist uprising in Berlin; the government relied on right-wing Freikorps to brutally crush it, setting a precedent of political bloodshed.

Hyperinflation (1923): Triggered by the French occupation of the Ruhr and government passive resistance/money printing, the mark became worthless, destroying middle-class savings and creating economic panic.

Right-Wing Putschism and Assassinations (Own Knowledge): The Kapp Putsch (1920) forced the government to flee Berlin; nationalist death squads murdered key politicians (Walter Rathenau, Matthias Erzberger); and Hitler launched the Munich Putsch (1923).
questions.examiner_tips: Structure three distinct causal factors: communist insurrection (Spartacists), monetary collapse (Ruhr/hyperinflation), and right-wing nationalist terror/putschism.

questions.topic: Nazi Methods of Controlling the German People (1933–39)
questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: The police state / KT3.3: Controlling attitudes
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into Nazi methods of controlling the German people in the years 1933–1939?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Extract from a speech by Joseph Goebbels explaining that the goal of propaganda is to unite the whole nation behind the Führer through total media control. Source C: Secret police report detailing citizen denunciations and Gestapo arrests of individuals listening to foreign radio broadcasts.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Shows the ideological rationale and systematic scope of Nazi propaganda to achieve "Gleichschaltung" (coordination) across radio, press, and arts.
Source B Provenance: Speech by the Minister of Propaganda himself; authoritative statement of regime intention, though claiming greater popular unity than existed in reality.
Source C Utility: Provides direct evidence of the police state in operation, revealing that surveillance relied heavily on voluntary denunciations by ordinary citizens.
Source C Provenance: Internal confidential Gestapo file; highly reliable record of routine enforcement and terror.
questions.examiner_tips: Assess both propaganda (Source B) and police terror/denunciation (Source C). Evaluate how nature, origin, and purpose shape their usefulness.

questions.topic: Nazi Methods of Control: Propaganda vs Terror
questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: The police state / KT3.3: Controlling attitudes
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about Nazi methods of controlling the German people in the years 1933–1939. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 argues that propaganda, censorship, and popular consensus were the primary methods of control, successfully winning over the hearts and minds of the German people.
Interpretation 2 argues that control was maintained fundamentally through terror, the Gestapo, concentration camps, and the omnipresent threat of denunciation.
questions.examiner_tips: State clearly the contrast: persuasion/propaganda (Interpretation 1) versus coercion/terror (Interpretation 2).

questions.topic: Nazi Methods of Control: Propaganda vs Terror
questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: The police state / KT3.3: Controlling attitudes
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about Nazi methods of controlling the German people in the years 1933–1939. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Differing Types of Evidence: The author of Interpretation 1 gave weight to official speeches, public media, and mass organisations (Source B), whereas Interpretation 2 prioritized police court records, Gestapo case files, and penal statistics (Source C).
Alternative: The historians examined different sections of society—one assessing compliant workers enjoying leisure perks, the other investigating non-conformists targeted by the SS.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that the interpretations differ because one author focused on Goebbels’ propaganda machine while the other focused on Himmler’s police state.

questions.topic: Nazi Control: Terror and Intimidation vs Popular Propaganda and Consent
questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: The police state / KT3.3: Controlling attitudes
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about Nazi methods of controlling the German people in the years 1933–1939? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Terror and the Police State): SS under Himmler and Gestapo under Heydrich operated outside the law; concentration camps (Dachau, Sachsenhausen); People’s Court; Blockleiter network created fear that any critical word would lead to arrest; trade unions abolished.

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Propaganda and Popular Consent): Control of radio (Volksempfänger), cinema, press, and rallies; genuine popular support created by economic recovery (autobahns, full employment) and foreign policy triumphs (Rhineland, Anschluss); social programmes like Strength through Joy (KdF).

Conclusion / Synthesis: Terror and propaganda were two sides of the same coin: propaganda created a loyal consensus among the majority, while terror ruthlessly eliminated any minority that refused to conform.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain the symbiotic relationship between "carrot" (propaganda/economic perks) and "stick" (Gestapo/concentration camps). Conclude with a strong, nuanced verdict.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The challenges of 1923: hyperinflation
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about the impact of hyperinflation in Germany in 1923.
indicative_content: Inference 1: Money lost its value so rapidly that everyday commerce broke down completely. Supporting detail: Source A recounts prices doubling within hours and people carrying wheelbarrows of cash.
Inference 2: Ordinary citizens were reduced to desperation, poverty, and barter. Supporting detail: text describes families exchanging heirlooms and watches for basic food supplies.
questions.examiner_tips: State two inferences regarding total currency collapse and human misery, supported by specific phrases from Source A.

questions.topic: Growth in Support for the Nazis (1929–32)
questions.spec_topic: KT2.3: The growth in support for the Nazis, 1929–32
questions.question_text: Explain why support for the Nazi party grew in the years 1929–1932.
questions.stimulus:
• the Wall Street Crash (1929) and the Great Depression
• Hitler’s speeches
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: The Wall Street Crash & Great Depression: US recalled Dawes Plan loans; German industrial output collapsed, banks failed, and unemployment rocketed to 6 million by 1932; Weimar coalitions failed to agree on welfare cuts, creating voter desperation.

Hitler’s Oratorical Appeal and Campaigning: Flown across Germany on the "Hitler over Germany" aeroplane campaign; delivered dynamic speeches offering simple solutions, scapegoating Jews and Weimar politicians, and promising "Work and Bread".

Broad Social Appeal and Fear of Communism (Own Knowledge): The SA projected discipline and order against communist street violence; the Nazis tailored propaganda to distinct groups—promising farmers agricultural subsidies, the middle classes protection against Bolshevism, and big industrialists anti-trade union stability.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain how the economic catalyst (Depression) interacted with political campaigning (Hitler’s speeches) and anti-communist fear to broaden the Nazi voting coalition.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.4: Opposition, resistance and conformity: youth opposition
questions.question_text: Explain why there was opposition from some young people towards the Nazis in the years 1933–1939.
questions.stimulus:
• the Edelweiss Pirates
• the Swing Youth
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: The Edelweiss Pirates: Working-class youths who rebelled against rigid military regimentation of the Hitler Youth; wore check shirts, went on unchaperoned camping hikes, sang anti-Nazi songs, and attacked Hitler Youth patrols.

The Swing Youth: Middle-class youths who rejected Nazi racial and cultural puritanism; embraced banned American jazz/swing music, danced in clubs, grew their hair long, and flaunted British clothing fashions.

Resentment of Compulsion and Indoctrination (Own Knowledge): From 1936 the Hitler Youth Law made membership virtually compulsory (1939 compulsory for all aged 10-18); many teenagers resented constant drilling, repetitive propaganda, and loss of personal freedom.
questions.examiner_tips: Distinguish between cultural rebellion (Swing Youth) and active defiance/street conflict (Edelweiss Pirates), explaining the underlying resentment of regimentation.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.3: Employment and living standards
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into people’s living standards in Nazi Germany in the years 1933–1939?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Promotional brochure for the Strength through Joy (KdF) cruise liner Wilhelm Gustloff advertising affordable holiday cruises for factory workers. Source C: Secret report by German social investigators noting rising food prices, longer working hours (up to 49 hours/week), and rationing of dairy products.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Provides evidence of state-subsidised leisure benefits, showing how the regime rewarded compliant workers with cruises, theatre tickets, and sports facilities.
Source B Provenance: Official propaganda produced by Robert Ley’s German Labour Front (DAF); glamorises luxury perks that only a minority of workers actually experienced.
Source C Utility: Gives detailed evidence of falling real wages for non-armaments workers, rising cost of living, longer hours, and trade unions being replaced by the DAF.
Source C Provenance: Confidential underground economic report; highly valuable for exposing the hidden erosion of workers’ purchasing power.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the publicised perks of Strength through Joy with the daily reality of longer hours, wage ceilings, and food shortages.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.3: Employment and living standards
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about people’s living standards in Nazi Germany in the years 1933–1939. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 suggests that living standards genuinely improved under the Nazis through full employment, KdF leisure rewards, and the Volkswagen scheme.
Interpretation 2 suggests that living standards deteriorated, as workers lost trade union rights, endured longer working hours, suffered wage freezes, and faced rising food prices.
questions.examiner_tips: Identify the clear difference: material improvement and leisure perks vs loss of worker freedom and declining real living conditions.

questions.spec_topic: KT4.3: Employment and living standards
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about people’s living standards in Nazi Germany in the years 1933–1939. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Focus / Criteria: Interpretation 1 looked at employment totals and official DAF leisure records (Source B), whereas Interpretation 2 examined real wages, working hours, and food price inflation (Source C).
Different groups of workers: Armaments workers enjoyed higher pay and bonuses, whereas consumer-goods workers suffered declining wages and shortages.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that the authors prioritised different indicators: leisure/employment perks vs real purchasing power and working hours.

questions.topic: Living Standards: Genuine Improvement or Exploitation of the Working Class?
questions.spec_topic: KT4.3: Employment and living standards
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about people’s living standards in Nazi Germany in the years 1933–1939? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Exploitation and Lower Standards): Trade unions abolished (May 1933); strikes banned; Labour Front (DAF) controlled workers; average working hours rose from 43 hours/week (1933) to 47+ hours (1939); real wages only matched 1928 levels by 1938; Volkswagen (Kdf-Wagen) savings stamps produced zero cars for workers as production switched to military vehicles.

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Gains and Security): Unemployment dropped from 6 million to virtually zero; wages were regular; Strength through Joy (KdF) took over 10 million people on holidays/cruises; Beauty of Labour (SdA) improved ventilation, lighting, and canteens in workplaces.

Conclusion / Synthesis: Workers traded their political and economic freedom for guaranteed employment. While living standards improved relative to the depths of the 1932 Great Depression, they did not surpass the late Weimar Golden Years, and gains were subordinated to rearmament.
questions.examiner_tips: Structure a thorough comparison using exact data (working hours, wage levels, KdF statistics). Reach a clear, reasoned judgement.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.4: Opposition, resistance and conformity
questions.question_text: Give two things you can infer from Source A about how the Nazi Party dealt with opposition in the years 1933–1939.
questions.stimulus: Source A: From a speech made by Pastor Niemöller in 1946 ("First they came for the communists... then the trade unionists... then the Jews... then they came for me").
indicative_content: Inference 1: The Nazis systematically eliminated opposition groups one by one to prevent united collective resistance. Supporting detail: Source A lists targeting communists, then trade unionists, then Jews, then church leaders sequentially.

Inference 2: The regime’s terror was so effective that ordinary Germans were intimidated into silence until no defenders remained. Supporting detail: text emphasizes "I did not speak out... and there was no one left to speak for me".
questions.examiner_tips: State two inferences regarding sequential targeting and the atmosphere of fear that silenced bystanders, quoting Niemöller’s speech.

questions.topic: Changes in the Position of Women (1924–39)
questions.spec_topic: KT1.4: Changes in the position of women / KT4.1: Nazi policies towards women
questions.question_text: Explain why there were changes in the position of women in society in the years 1924–1939.
questions.stimulus:
• jobs for women in Weimar Germany
• Nazi policies on family
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: Weimar "New Woman" (1924–29): The Weimar Constitution gave women the vote (Article 109) and equal civil rights; female employment expanded in white-collar sectors (teaching, secretarial, medicine); women enjoyed greater social freedom in fashion, cosmetics, and unchaperoned leisure.

Nazi Family Policies (1933–37): The regime sought to reverse Weimar progress, promoting "Children, Kitchen, Church"; introduced marriage loans (up to 1,000 marks), the Mother’s Cross, and anti-abortion laws; barred women from civil service and judiciary.

Rearmament Reversal (Own Knowledge, 1937–39): As the Four-Year Plan caused acute factory labour shortages, the regime was forced to reverse its stay-at-home policy; introduced compulsory Duty Year (Pflichtjahr) for unmarried women, leading to 14.6 million women working by 1939.
questions.examiner_tips: Demonstrate change over time: liberal emancipation under Weimar, conservative restriction under early Nazi rule, and pragmatic economic reversal by 1939.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.4: How Hitler became Chancellor, 1932–33
questions.question_text: Explain why Hitler became Chancellor in 1933.
questions.stimulus:
• President Hindenburg
• elections in 1932
• You must also use information of your own.
indicative_content: President Hindenburg and Elite Conspiracy: Hindenburg initially despised Hitler as a "Bohemian corporal", but Franz von Papen persuaded him that appointing Hitler with Papen as Vice-Chancellor would tame the Nazis while providing a parliamentary majority.

Elections in 1932 (Electoral Mandate): In July 1932, the Nazis won 230 seats (37.3%), making them the largest party in the Reichstag; democratic government collapsed into rule by presidential decree under Article 48.

Fear of Communism and SA Presence (Own Knowledge): The Wall Street Crash created 6 million unemployed; industrialists and middle classes backed Hitler out of fear of a communist revolution; the 400,000-strong SA projected strength and order.
questions.examiner_tips: Integrate the role of Hindenburg/Papen’s backstairs intrigue with the 1932 electoral breakthrough and elite fear of communist uprising.

questions.topic: Problems Faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The challenges of 1923
questions.question_text: How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into the problems faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923?
questions.stimulus: Source B: Photograph of French soldiers guarding a Ruhr coal mine and confronting striking German miners (1923). Source C: Contemporary diary entry describing soaring prices, carrying bundles of million-mark notes, and fear of starvation in Berlin.
indicative_content: Source B Utility: Documents the foreign military crisis triggered by the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr, showing passive resistance and the loss of Germany’s industrial heartland.
Source B Provenance: Contemporary photographic evidence of foreign troops on German soil; useful for demonstrating the national humiliation and industrial disruption.
Source C Utility: Provides direct personal evidence of the hyperinflation crisis, showing how the currency collapse disrupted daily survival and destroyed middle-class savings.
Source C Provenance: Private diary from 1923; highly credible for emotional and domestic reality, free from state censorship.
questions.examiner_tips: Assess foreign occupation/loss of production (Source B) alongside domestic monetary collapse/starvation (Source C). Evaluate content and provenance.

questions.topic: Problems Faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The challenges of 1923
questions.question_text: Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the problems faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923. What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.
indicative_content: Main difference: Interpretation 1 suggests that the primary danger facing the Weimar Republic in 1923 was economic collapse caused by hyperinflation and passive resistance.

Interpretation 2 suggests that the greatest threat was political and military extremism, as right-wing and left-wing radicals (such as Hitler in the Munich Putsch) attempted armed rebellion to overthrow the state.
questions.examiner_tips: State the difference clearly: economic catastrophe (Interpretation 1) vs political insurrection/putschism (Interpretation 2).

questions.topic: Problems Faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The challenges of 1923
questions.question_text: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about the problems faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923. You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.
indicative_content: Different Source Material: Interpretation 1 drew upon economic records and accounts of daily starvation during hyperinflation (Source C), whereas Interpretation 2 drew upon police and court records of armed putsches (Ruhr confrontations in Source B and the Munich Putsch).
Different historical emphasis: One author evaluates socio-economic stability; the other evaluates constitutional survival and armed insurrection.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain that the historians emphasized different dimensions of the 1923 crisis: financial breakdown vs paramilitary rebellion.

questions.topic: The 1923 Crisis: Economic Ruin vs Political Overthrow
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The challenges of 1923
questions.question_text: How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the problems faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923? Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
indicative_content: Supporting Interpretation 2 (Political and Military Threat): Armed rebellion threatened the state: the Bavarian government under Kahr defied Berlin; Hitler launched the Munich Beer Hall Putsch (Nov 1923); left-wing uprisings occurred in Saxony and Thuringia; General von Seeckt declared "the army stands behind me".

Supporting Interpretation 1 (Economic Ruin): Hyperinflation wiped out middle-class savings, bonds, and pensions; printing presses ran 24/7; barter replaced currency; food riots broke out; workers demanded wages paid daily; international credit was ruined.

Conclusion / Synthesis: The economic catastrophe of hyperinflation was the root cause that triggered the political rebellions; Stresemann’s appointment and decisive currency reform (Rentenmark) defused both threats, proving the republic was resilient enough to survive.
questions.examiner_tips: Provide a sustained evaluation linking the French occupation and hyperinflation directly to the outbreak of political insurrections. Award up to 4 marks for SPaG.
